lead: A gas turbine is a steady-flow engine: compress air, burn fuel to heat it, expand it through a turbine, and reject the rest. The Brayton cycle models this loop with four processes, two isentropic and two at constant pressure. Its efficiency depends on the pressure ratio, not on the volume ratio used in piston engines. The Stirling cycle is different: two isotherms and two constant-volume steps, with a regenerator that stores and returns heat. Its ideal efficiency equals the Carnot value. Both cycles appear in aircraft engines, power plants, and solar or waste-heat engines.
prereq: You need: the steady flow energy equation from Unit 2, and the air-standard assumptions and Otto cycle from Chapter 6.1 and Chapter 6.2.

blocks.text: The Brayton cycle is the gas-turbine cycle. Air is compressed from state 1 to 2, heated at constant pressure to 3, expanded through a turbine to 4, and cooled at constant pressure back to 1. Processes 1→2 and 3→4 are isentropic in the air-standard model. Some syllabi call this the Joule cycle or the constant-pressure cycle.
r<sub>p</sub> = p<sub>2</sub>/p<sub>1</sub> = p<sub>3</sub>/p<sub>4</sub>,   T<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = T<sub>3</sub>/T<sub>4</sub> = r<sub>p</sub><sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>
blocks.where: r<sub>p</sub> is the pressure ratio (no unit); p is absolute pressure in kPa or bar; T is absolute temperature in K; γ = c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> is the specific heat ratio, about 1.4 for air.

blocks.text: The work terms per unit mass of air follow. The back work ratio bwr is the part of turbine work that drives the compressor.

w<sub>c</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T<sub>2</sub> − T<sub>1</sub>),   w<sub>t</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T<sub>3</sub> − T<sub>4</sub>),   w<sub>net</sub> = w<sub>t</sub> − w<sub>c</sub>,   bwr = w<sub>c</sub>/w<sub>t</sub>,   q<sub>in</sub> = c<sub>p</sub>(T<sub>3</sub> − T<sub>2</sub>),   η = w<sub>net</sub>/q<sub>in</sub> = 1 − 1/r<sub>p</sub><sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup>
blocks.where: w<sub>c</sub> is compressor work in kJ/kg; w<sub>t</sub> is turbine work in kJ/kg; w<sub>net</sub> is net work in kJ/kg; bwr is a fraction; q<sub>in</sub> is heat added in kJ/kg; c<sub>p</sub> is specific heat at constant pressure in kJ/kg·K; η is thermal efficiency (fraction).

blocks.text: A real gas turbine is an open cycle. Fresh air enters the compressor, fuel burns in the combustion chamber, and exhaust leaves. The closed cycle replaces combustion by an external heater and cooler, so the same air repeats the loop. A regenerator uses hot exhaust to preheat air after the compressor; it saves fuel, but the simple η formula above ignores it.

The ideal efficiency depends only on pressure ratio and γ. For air γ = 1.4. At r<sub>p</sub> = 8, η = 1 − 1/1.811 = 0.448, or 44.8%. A higher r<sub>p</sub> gives a higher η, but the compressor exit temperature also rises.

Raising T<sub>3</sub> at fixed r<sub>p</sub> leaves this ideal η unchanged. It raises w<sub>net</sub> because turbine work grows while compressor work stays fixed. The back work ratio falls. Turbine inlet temperatures of 1200–1500 K are used to get more work per kg of air, not to change the ideal efficiency formula. Real efficiency also falls due to component losses.

sections.h3: Stirling cycle: two isotherms, two constant-volume steps

blocks.text: The Stirling cycle has four processes. 1→2: isothermal compression at T<sub>C</sub>, with heat q<sub>out</sub> rejected to the cold sink. 2→3: constant-volume heating; the regenerator gives up stored heat. 3→4: isothermal expansion at T<sub>H</sub>, with heat q<sub>in</sub> taken from the external source. 4→1: constant-volume cooling; the regenerator stores heat from the gas.

The two constant-volume steps exchange heat internally. A good regenerator stores most of the heat from 4→1 and returns it in 2→3. Then external heat enters only during 3→4, at T<sub>H</sub>, and leaves only during 1→2, at T<sub>C</sub>. The ideal cycle therefore has the Carnot efficiency.

blocks.where: T<sub>C</sub> is the cold-space absolute temperature in K; T<sub>H</sub> is the hot-space absolute temperature in K; η is the ideal thermal efficiency (fraction).

blocks.text: A Stirling engine needs an external heat source and a good regenerator. It can use solar heat, biomass, or waste heat, because the working gas never mixes with the fuel. Real efficiency is lower due to friction, imperfect regeneration, and finite-speed processes. A poor regenerator wastes the constant-volume heat and drops η below Carnot.

figure.caption: The loop runs compressor, heater, turbine, cooler. State 1 is compressor inlet, 2 compressor exit, 3 turbine inlet, and 4 turbine exit; every heat transfer is at constant pressure.

spec.aria: Four blocks in a closed loop: compressor, heater, turbine and cooler, with state numbers 1 to 4 on the connecting lines.

examples.question: A simple ideal Brayton cycle has pressure ratio r<sub>p</sub> = 8. The compressor inlet temperature is 300 K and the turbine inlet temperature is 1200 K. Take c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4. Find T<sub>2</sub>, T<sub>4</sub>, compressor work, turbine work, net work, heat added, and cycle efficiency.
steps: Compute the temperature ratio: x = r<sub>p</sub><sup>(γ−1)/γ</sup> = 8<sup>0.4/1.4</sup> = 8<sup>0.2857</sup> = 1.811.
examples.answer: T<sub>2</sub> = 543.4 K, T<sub>4</sub> = 662.5 K, w<sub>c</sub> = 244.6 kJ/kg, w<sub>t</sub> = 540.2 kJ/kg, w<sub>net</sub> = 295.6 kJ/kg, q<sub>in</sub> = 659.9 kJ/kg, and η = 0.448 (44.8%).
examples.check:
rp = 8.0
T1 = 300.0
T3 = 1200.0
cp = 1.005
g = 1.4
x = rp ** ((g - 1) / g)
T2 = round(T1 * x, 1)
T4 = round(T3 / x, 1)
wc = round(cp * (T2 - T1), 1)
wt = round(cp * (T3 - T4), 1)
wn = round(wt - wc, 1)
qin = round(cp * (T3 - T2), 1)
eta = round(wn / qin, 3)
print(round(x, 3))
print(T2)
print(T4)
print(wc)
print(wt)
print(wn)
print(qin)
print(eta)

traps: Using a volume ratio, V<sub>1</sub>/V<sub>2</sub>, inside a Brayton cycle. It is a steady-flow cycle; the key ratio is r<sub>p</sub> = p<sub>2</sub>/p<sub>1</sub>.
Expecting ideal efficiency to rise when T<sub>3</sub> is raised at fixed r<sub>p</sub>. It stays the same; only w<sub>net</sub> and the back work ratio change.
Calling w<sub>c</sub>/w<sub>t</sub> the efficiency. That is the back work ratio; η = (w<sub>t</sub> − w<sub>c</sub>)/q<sub>in</sub>.
Treating the constant-volume heat transfers in a Stirling cycle as external heat. In the ideal cycle they pass through the regenerator, so q<sub>in</sub> is taken only at T<sub>H</sub>.
Writing Stirling efficiency as a function of pressure ratio. The ideal Stirling efficiency is 1 − T<sub>C</sub>/T<sub>H</sub>, the Carnot value.

quiz.q: List the four processes of an ideal Brayton cycle in order.
quiz.a: 1→2 isentropic compression, 2→3 constant-pressure heat addition, 3→4 isentropic expansion, 4→1 constant-pressure heat rejection.

quiz.q: Why is the pressure ratio r<sub>p</sub> used for the Brayton cycle instead of the compression ratio used for the Otto cycle?
quiz.a: Brayton is a steady-flow cycle. The same air flows through compressor and turbine, so the pressure ratio fixes the temperature ratio. A volume ratio belongs to a closed piston device.

quiz.q: For air with γ = 1.4, find T<sub>2</sub> when T<sub>1</sub> = 300 K and r<sub>p</sub> = 4.
At fixed r<sub>p</sub> = 8, T<sub>3</sub> is raised from 1200 K to 1400 K. What happens to ideal η and to w<sub>net</sub>?
quiz.a: Ideal η stays 0.448 because it depends only on r<sub>p</sub> and γ. w<sub>net</sub> rises because turbine work increases while compressor work is unchanged.

quiz.q: What is the job of the regenerator in a Stirling cycle?
quiz.a: It stores heat rejected during 4→1 and returns it during 2→3. This internal exchange lets external heat enter only at T<sub>H</sub>, giving Carnot efficiency in the ideal case.

quiz.q: Write the ideal efficiency of a Stirling cycle between T<sub>H</sub> and T<sub>C</sub>.
A Stirling engine works between 900 K and 300 K. Find its ideal efficiency.
Why does a real Stirling engine need a good regenerator and an external heat source?
quiz.a: The external source supplies q<sub>in</sub> at T<sub>H</sub>; without it the cycle cannot run. The regenerator must return most of the constant-volume heat. A poor regenerator loses that heat, so more external heat is needed and efficiency falls below Carnot.

beyond: Not for the exam. Practical gas turbines add regeneration, intercooling and reheat, and cool the blades with bleed air. Combined gas-steam plants use the hot exhaust in a Rankine bottoming cycle, reaching higher efficiency. Stirling engines appear in solar dish systems and space power because they need only an external temperature difference.
